## Start with a specific question

**LeetCode 149 — Max Points on a Line.** We will reason from a very small example rather than introduce a complicated notation first.

## What the obvious approach overlooks

Computing a floating-point slope for each pair looks simple but vertical lines and rounding create dangerous cases.

## One simple idea

Use orientation or a normalised integer direction. The cross product tells whether three 2D points are collinear without dividing by x differences.

Before reading symbols, explain the intended operation aloud. If you can say which information is saved and which work is avoided, you have the core intuition.

## Formula and immediate translation

$$
(b_x-a_x)(c_y-a_y)-(b_y-a_y)(c_x-a_x)=0
$$

**Symbols and notation:** a,b,c are 2D points; the x/y subscripts select their coordinates. The left-hand side is the signed two-dimensional cross product of vectors b−a and c−a.

**Insert actual numbers:** For a=(0,0), b=(2,2), c=(3,3), compute (2)(3)−(2)(3)=6−6=0: all three lie on one line. If c=(3,4), the result becomes 8−6=2, so they are not collinear.

This numerical calculation is essential: the expression must mean the same thing when evaluated by hand and when written in code.

## Why the mathematics leads to an algorithm

A zero determinant means the displacement vectors are linearly dependent, hence they point along the same line (allowing appropriate degenerate handling).

This argument is the bridge between 'the equation looks plausible' and 'the result is correct for all inputs satisfying the assumptions'.

## Make the idea executable

Start with the numerical example above and write a tiny function or test that reproduces it. For comparison, examine the [original executable patterns library](../examples/patterns.mjs). This topic's main challenge is its mathematical invariant rather than framework setup.

## Complexity and correctness boundaries

**Work bound:** O(1) orientation test per triple, but the full max-points problem often needs O(n²) pair processing.

**Counterexample or limitation:** A cross product of zero also occurs for repeated points, so duplicates need separate treatment. In fixed-width integer languages the products can overflow.

Always declare the input domain first. For example, a modulus must be positive, a probability denominator nonzero and a character indexing convention fixed. Many seemingly clever solutions fail because these conditions were never stated.
